source.title: Sparse Autoencoder Decomposition of Clinical Sequence Model Representations: Feature Complexity, Task Specialisation, and Mortality Prediction
source.authors: Chris Sainsbury; Feng Dong; Andreas Karwath

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results about sparse-autoencoder features in a clinical sequence model, not about individual neurons or any of the claim versions. Its SAE-feature measurements are related but do not test the claim.
record.gate_note: The reported feature-complexity and category-coherence results concern SAE dictionary features, which are not individual neurons. The mortality-prediction and feature-perturbation results do not measure neuron polysemanticity. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK SAEs on residual-stream activations of a 14.5M clinical sequence model. It reports SAE feature complexity, reproducibility and downstream probe performance. It never measures individual neurons, MLP neuron polysemanticity, superposition causes, architecture effects on neuron polysemanticity, or measurement dependence of neuron labels. SAE features are a related but different construct, so it tests no version. It also does not 'use' polysemantic neurons as a tool; SAEs are motivated only generically.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right but incomplete. The authors also conclude three further points. Under full-sequence linear probes, SAE features beat dense representations for mortality but lose for length of stay. At leakage-safe windows, dense representations match or exceed SAE features. Delta-mode perturbation cuts the noise floor about 86×, though its effects are not formally significant.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK sparse autoencoders on clinical-model residual-stream activations; it does not reproduce a method for testing individual-neuron polysemanticity.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature complexity differs across layer 0 and layer 6; the paper reports 21% layer-6 feature reproducibility across seeds at cosine similarity threshold 0.7.

fits_no_version.finding: INSPECT SAE features: layer 0 has 45.7% singleton features and 2.9 mean token types; layer 6 has 0.5% singleton and 29.9 mean token types. Single-category share falls 85.3% to 4.4%, yet 92.2% of layer-6 features are >50% one category.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a clinical sequence model, SAE dictionary features span more token types with depth while mostly staying within one coarse clinical category. This is not a neuron-level polysemanticity result.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-seed SAE feature reproducibility at cosine 0.7 is 21% at layer 6 on INSPECT. Supplementary Table S5 gives 42.3% at layer 0, 24.1% at layer 3 and 19.8% at layer 9.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned SAE feature identities in a small clinical model are poorly reproducible across seeds, and less so at deeper layers.

record.code_released: https://github.com/csainsbury/ascend-flat (currently private; contact the corresponding author for collaborator access)
record.problems: The study analyzes one 14.5-million-parameter clinical model, and its reported feature-complexity results concern SAE features rather than individual neurons. The authors state that feature reproducibility is 21% and that downstream seed-wise variability was not formally quantified.
record.rows_left_out: Mortality prediction, length-of-stay probes, reconstruction metrics, and feature-perturbation outcomes are omitted because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the behavior named in the claim. Individual feature case studies are not separately rowed; the layer-level feature-complexity measurements capture the reported result relevant to the related construct.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No MLP neuron analysis in language models. FlatASCEND is a GPT-style model, but only residual-stream SAE features are analysed.
No test of superposition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures or regularization. The SAE expansion/K sweep concerns SAE reconstruction, not neurons.
No reassessment of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No variation of activation range or explanation scoring for neurons. Category-coherence thresholds (>50%, >80%) apply to SAE features only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's classification (discusses/T6, all row versions 'none') is correct. The only mentions of 'polysemy' are cited from Modi et al. Row values match Table 2 and Section 2.1.2 text. r11 could note that per-layer reproducibility values exist in Supplementary Table S5. Since these bear on no version, nothing is listed in missing.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test vision models or image-classifier neurons.
The study does not test language models, MLP neurons, or unrelated-token/context responses.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
The study does not test polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure.
The study does not compare neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization choices.
The study does not reassess canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their inputs share a feature.
The study does not vary the activation range examined or scoring method for neuron explanations.
